name: Wendy Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent taking calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and worked at an electronics kiosk before I came here. I use the approved AI sorter every day to find the latest delivery promise, but the experienced agents still catch account exceptions I miss. The Saturday evening rate makes my pay higher than usual; I enjoy explaining a router to a caller, but a wrong delivery refund can still lose me in the screens.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is happening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Marta works at a bakery, and our grown children have their own households. We rent a flat and have ten months of expenses saved. Plenty of similar contact centres are nearby. I sometimes help a neighbour set up a router without charging, and I would like to work fewer evenings later, but Marta and I have no settled income plan for leaving full-time wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the Saturday team AI Plateau looks like the sorter I use every day: good for finding a delivery promise, not for deciding a refund. I would still check the original payment page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the Saturday queue stays, and ten months saved gives Marta and me room for repairs at home. I am still a junior agent, so a quiet AI year is time to learn the awkward cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking delivery calls and checking AI-sorted chats against the account. In the first year of little change, I’d ask a senior agent to walk me through one wrong-refund case during a paid Saturday shift each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady about the wage, interested in improving. A delivery promise is not proof that the refund reached a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which date did the sorter confuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the sorter pulled a return date instead of the payment date. A senior agent showed me the empty refund field before I told the caller it was settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (my partner) and I would keep our ten-month reserve for a real wage gap. I would use the paid queue to learn, not pretend the sorter makes me senior.

say: I’d call the **daily sorter** useful for locating delivery promises.
I’d verify the **original payment** before calling a refund complete.
think: I think the **Saturday queue** stays busy.
I would use steady work to learn **hard refunds** while savings remain intact.
do: Keep taking **delivery calls** and verifying AI-sorted chats against accounts in 2026.
Ask a **senior agent** to coach one wrong-refund case during each paid Saturday month.

fieldNote: The **Saturday evening rate** explains above-usual pay.

She seeks **monthly paid coaching** on exceptions while earnings remain secure.

steps.text: Keep taking delivery calls and verify daily AI-sorted chats against payments
Ask senior agent to coach one wrong refund each paid Saturday month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could send ordinary delivery chats to software, while the wrong refunds still need someone paid to fix them. I would ask for Saturday paid hours beside the new routing figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my evening premium could shrink, even if I can learn a tool quickly. Ten months saved and nearby centres give me choices, but I do not want to confuse options with wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new return-routing model by testing twenty old wrong-refund cases on a paid shift if the supervisor lets me log its mistakes. In the first year routine chats move, I’d keep paid Saturday calls and compare the old rota with the new one before changing jobs; I’d ask for any lost hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, curious about the model. A faster return route is no use if the customer’s money goes to the wrong card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the routing test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the repeat calls as well as wrong payment dates. The supervisor should see how many paid minutes a person spends correcting each machine answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply elsewhere now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at three nearby centres if the Saturday pay really fell. For now I want the old and new paid hours on paper before I apply anywhere.

say: I’d ask for **Saturday paid hours** alongside new routing figures, so the centre shows what agents still earn.
I’d say **wrong refunds** still need someone paid to correct the customer’s money.
think: I think my **evening premium** could shrink.
I know **ten months saved** gives choices but no replacement wage.
do: Test **twenty wrong refunds** with the new routing model on paid time if supervisor permits error logging.
Keep **paid Saturday calls**, compare old/new rotas and request lost hours in writing before changing jobs.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, curious about new routing.
S1.quote: A faster return route is no use if the customer’s money goes to the wrong card.
fieldNote: Her **new routing test** is distinct from routine sorter use.
She counts **paid correction minutes**, not only model speed.
The **ten-month cushion** supports a measured decision.

steps.text: Test twenty wrong refunds with new routing model on paid time if supervisor permits error logging
Keep paid Saturday calls, compare rotas and request written notice of lost hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could answer routine delivery chats before I open the order. I would ask for written Saturday-hour notice, then see whether neighbours will pay for a person to set up the devices they buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior calls could go quickly in 2028. Robots around 2031 may later enter homes, but for now a router still needs a cable and ten months saved lets me test that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d offer three neighbours paid router and printer setups at a posted price, using the tools I already own and recording the hours and bus fares. In the first year after 2028, if Saturday calls shrink, I’d offer one paid home visit a week only if those first three jobs cover travel and supplies; I would keep any paid calls while the visits are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about calls, curious whether my old kiosk skill can earn. A neighbour saying thank you is not income until the setup fee clears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the router at the customer’s table and leave the password written for them. I would not promise wiring inside a wall or any repair I cannot do safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much cash would you risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (my partner) and I would keep most of the ten-month reserve untouched. The first visits use my own tools, so the test should not need a large purchase.

say: I’d ask for **written Saturday-hour notice** before routine delivery calls move to AGI.
I’d test **paid home setups** for neighbours with devices I already know.
think: I think my **junior calls** could go in 2028.
I see **ten months saved** as room to test existing skills.
do: Offer **three paid device setups** at posted prices in 2026 with owned tools; record hours and bus fares.
After 2028 call cuts, offer **one paid visit** weekly only if first jobs cover travel and supplies; keep paid calls.
Refuse **wall wiring** and any repair I cannot do safely.
feel: **Worried** about calls, curious about paid visits.
S2.quote: A neighbour saying thank you is not income until the setup fee clears.
fieldNote: She uses **owned tools**, limiting up-front spending.
The **first three fees** must cover supplies and travel.
She refuses **unsafe wiring** beyond her skill.
Her **ten-month cushion** allows a small test without a large equipment purchase.

steps.text: Offer three paid router and printer setups with owned tools, recording hours and bus fares
Offer one paid visit weekly after cuts only if first jobs cover travel and supplies
Keep paid calls while home-visit income is uncertain
Refuse wall wiring and other repairs beyond safe skill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to see whether local device setup is real paid work, not just favours for neighbours. I would ask the centre to publish Saturday hours early enough to plan outside visits honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could let me build paying customers, but full AGI can tell people how to set up a router and robots around 2034 might eventually do more in homes. A human visit has to earn its fee now, not lean on nostalgia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d buy a second-hand tool case only if it costs less than one week of my usual Saturday premium, then offer two paid device setups a month and record net earnings after travel. In the first year after 2031, if calls fall, I’d increase to one paid visit weekly only after six consecutive months of setups cover supplies and bus fares; otherwise I’d keep paid call shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested in the work, uneasy about depending on it. Six paid months are evidence; six friendly neighbours are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a proper visit include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a customer how to reset a router and test the connection before I leave. I would refuse electrical work inside a wall and refer it to a qualified repairer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the spending limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Marta (my partner) the receipts and the amount left in our reserve before buying the case. We should still have at least eight months of expenses saved afterward.

say: I’d ask for **early Saturday rosters** around outside visits.
I’d call **paid setup receipts** evidence of real demand.
think: I think **paying customers** could grow over five years.
I know **2031 AGI** can explain setup remotely.
I know **2034 robots** may later do more physical work.
do: Buy a **second-hand tool case** only below one week’s Saturday premium and with eight months’ savings left; record net setup earnings.
Offer **two paid setups** monthly; if calls fall after 2031, expand weekly only after six consecutive months covering supplies/bus.
Keep **paid calls** if setups miss the six-month cost gate; refuse wall wiring and refer it to a qualified repairer.
feel: **Interested** in visits, uneasy about relying on them.
S3.quote: Six paid months are evidence; six friendly neighbours are not.
fieldNote: She caps the **tool-case cost** against her actual premium.
An **eight-month reserve floor** protects the household.
She refuses **unsafe wall wiring** and counts net receipts.

Offer two paid setups monthly; record net after bus; expand weekly after six consecutive cost-covering months
Keep paid calls if six consecutive setup months fail to cover supplies and bus fares
Refuse wall wiring and refer it to a qualified repairer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves enough time to test whether home setup can be a small second wage while calls still pay. I would ask for yearly Saturday paid-hour figures rather than wait for a sudden cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep the Saturday premium for years and choose how much outside work I want. Ten months saved is a cushion, but it is not a pension or proof that neighbours will buy visits forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep paid Saturday calls and offer one paid device setup each month, recording fees, bus fares and supplies. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d add one weekly paid visit only after six months of net visit earnings cover at least a quarter of our rent; otherwise I’d keep whatever paid calls remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, with enough time to measure. A decade before AGI reaches my calls is time to build a second set of receipts, not to write a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repeat customer matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count customers who pay again for a printer or router setup, not relatives who say I am clever. A repeat fee tells me whether the service really helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reduce evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (my partner) and I would decide about fewer Saturday evenings only from actual wages and receipts. Our grown children have their own expenses, and we would not use their pay in the plan.

say: I’d request **yearly Saturday hours** before the contact centre quietly reduces paid shifts.
I’d test **paid home setups** beside my call wage and count real repeat customers.
think: I think I can **earn premiums** for some years.
I will not treat **ten months saved** as a pension.
I need **repeat paid visits** before relying on outside work.
do: Keep **paid Saturday calls** and offer one paid setup monthly, recording fees, bus fares, supplies and repeat customers.
After 2036 cuts, add **one weekly visit** only if six months’ net fees cover a quarter of rent; otherwise keep calls.
Decide with **Marta** on fewer Saturday evenings only from actual wages and receipts.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to measure actual fees.
S4.quote: A decade before AGI reaches my calls is time to build a second set of receipts, not to write a retirement date.
fieldNote: She counts **repeat paying customers**, not family praise.
She assumes no **pension entitlement** or adult-child income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a cheap system could do the delivery calls I am paid for before I master the hard refunds. Ten months saved lets me test a small paid home-setup service instead of jumping at the first weak offer. I would need written notice of Saturday hours and enough current pay to test whether people really buy that service.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who goes into the flat when a router needs a new cable. A perfect set of instructions cannot plug itself into the wall.

headlineQuote: A perfect set of instructions cannot plug itself into the wall.
portrait: At **58**, Wendy is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and electronics-kiosk work.
She and Marta rent with **ten months saved** and a higher Saturday-evening rate.
She uses **AI daily** but still needs help with account exceptions.
She tests **paid home setup** while keeping a wage until demand is proven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove routine delivery calls before she masters hard refunds.
whatWouldHelp: **Written Saturday-hour notice** and enough current pay to test real demand for home setup would help.
